answer: (a) Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL). The algebraic sum of the currents meeting at a node (junction) at any instant is zero, i.e. total current entering a node = total current leaving it. Σ I = 0. It follows from conservation of charge: charge cannot accumulate at a node. Example: at a node with I1, I2 entering and I3, I4 leaving, I1 + I2 = I3 + I4.

Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL). The algebraic sum of all the voltage drops and EMFs around any closed loop (mesh) is zero. Σ V = 0, or Σ E = Σ IR. It follows from conservation of energy: a unit charge returns to the same potential after going once round a closed path. Sign convention: while traversing a loop, a rise in potential (−→+ through a source) is taken positive and a drop (current direction in a resistor) is taken negative. For a loop with source E and resistors R1, R2 in series: E − IR1 − IR2 = 0.

Electrical resistance. Resistance is the opposition offered by a material to the flow of current; R = V/I (ohm, Ω) and for a conductor R = ρl/A, where ρ is resistivity, l length and A area of cross-section.

Effect of temperature. (i) Conductors (metals): resistance increases with temperature because increased lattice vibration causes more collisions of free electrons; positive temperature coefficient: Rt = R0(1 + α0t). (ii) Semiconductors: resistance decreases with temperature because more covalent bonds break, producing more electron–hole pairs; negative temperature coefficient. (iii) Insulators: resistance decreases with temperature (negative coefficient) because more charge carriers are thermally released and insulation breaks down at high temperature. Alloys such as manganin, constantan have almost zero coefficient.

(b) Classification of elements. (i) Unilateral element: its v–i characteristic depends on the direction of current, e.g. diode, transistor. (ii) Bilateral element: has the same v–i relation for both directions of current, e.g. resistor, inductor, capacitor. (iii) Active element: supplies energy to the circuit, e.g. voltage and current sources, batteries. (iv) Passive element: absorbs or stores energy and cannot supply it, e.g. R, L, C. (v) Linear element: obeys superposition and homogeneity, v–i is a straight line through the origin (R, L, C with constant values); non-linear element: v–i is not a straight line, e.g. diode, thermistor, saturated iron-core inductor.

(c) Sources. An independent voltage source maintains a fixed terminal voltage whatever the current (symbol: circle with +/− or battery); an independent current source supplies a fixed current whatever the voltage (circle with an arrow). A dependent (controlled) source has its value controlled by a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit and is drawn as a diamond. Four types: VCVS (v = μvx), CCVS (v = r ix), VCCS (i = g vx), CCCS (i = β ix). They model transistors and op-amps.

(d) Inductor. v = L di/dt. Power p = vi = Li di/dt, so energy stored E = ∫0I Li di = ½LI². The inductor stores energy in its magnetic field; current cannot change instantaneously; it acts as a short circuit to DC in steady state.

Capacitor. i = C dv/dt. Power p = vi = Cv dv/dt, so E = ∫0V Cv dv = ½CV². It stores energy in the electric field; voltage across it cannot change instantaneously; it acts as an open circuit to DC in steady state.

answer: (a) Thevenin's theorem. Any linear, bilateral two-terminal active network can be replaced, as far as a load connected across its terminals is concerned, by a single voltage source Vth in series with a resistance Rth. Vth is the open-circuit voltage across the terminals and Rth is the resistance seen from the terminals with all independent sources deactivated.

Procedure. Step 1: remove the load RL and mark the terminals A and B. Step 2: calculate Vth = VAB (open circuit) by any method (KVL, voltage divider, nodal). Step 3: replace every independent voltage source by a short circuit and every current source by an open circuit (internal resistances remain); find Rth looking into A–B. Step 4: draw the equivalent circuit, reconnect RL and find IL = Vth/(Rth + RL).
Example. A 12 V source with R1 = 4 Ω in series, and R2 = 12 Ω across the output terminals A–B, load RL = 5 Ω. Vth = 12 × 12/(4 + 12) = 9 V. Rth = 4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω. IL = 9/(3 + 5) = 1.125 A.

(b) Norton's theorem. Any linear bilateral two-terminal active network can be replaced by a current source IN in parallel with a resistance RN. IN is the short-circuit current through the terminals and RN is the resistance seen from the terminals with sources deactivated (RN = Rth).

Procedure. Short the terminals A–B (remove load) and find Isc = IN; deactivate sources and find RN; the load current is IL = IN RN/(RN + RL) (current divider). For the above example IN = 12/4 = 3 A (R2 shorted), RN = 3 Ω, IL = 3 × 3/(3 + 5) = 1.125 A, the same result.

Duality. The Thevenin voltage source Vth with series Rth is converted to the Norton current source IN with parallel RN by source transformation: IN = Vth/Rth, RN = Rth, equivalently Vth = IN RN and Rth = Voc/Isc. Series ↔ parallel, voltage ↔ current, open-circuit ↔ short-circuit: the two models are duals and give identical terminal behaviour (not identical internal power dissipation).

answer: Statement. In a linear bilateral network containing more than one independent source, the current through (or voltage across) any element is the algebraic sum of the currents (voltages) produced by each source acting alone, with all the other independent sources replaced by their internal resistances.

Explanation. When one source acts, other ideal voltage sources are replaced by short circuits (V = 0) and other ideal current sources by open circuits (I = 0). Dependent sources are never deactivated; they remain in the circuit. The partial responses are added with proper regard to direction (sign).

Procedure. (1) Retain one source and deactivate the rest. (2) Calculate the required branch current I′ using series–parallel reduction or current divider. (3) Repeat for each remaining source to obtain I″, I‴ … (4) Add algebraically: I = I′ + I″ + I‴. Directions opposite to the assumed one are subtracted.

Example. Two sources E1 = 10 V (series R1 = 10 Ω) and E2 = 20 V (series R2 = 20 Ω) feed a common load R = 40 Ω. With E1 alone: Rtotal = 10 + (20 ∥ 40) = 23.33 Ω, I1 = 0.4286 A, load share = 0.4286 × 20/60 = 0.1429 A. With E2 alone: Rtotal = 20 + (10 ∥ 40) = 28 Ω, I2 = 0.7143 A, load share = 0.7143 × 10/50 = 0.1429 A. Both act in the same direction, so Iload = 0.1429 + 0.1429 = 0.2857 A.

Limitations. (i) It is applicable only to linear networks (R, L, C with constant values) that are bilateral; it fails for diodes, transistors, saturated iron-core elements. (ii) It cannot be applied directly to power, since P = I²R is a square (non-linear) function: P ≠ P′ + P″; one must first add the currents and then compute I²R. (iii) Dependent sources cannot be removed. (iv) It is lengthy for networks with many sources, so mesh/nodal analysis is preferred then. (v) Applies to voltage and current but the sources must be independent.

answer: Statement. A DC network delivers maximum power to a variable resistive load when the load resistance equals the Thevenin equivalent resistance of the network as seen from the load terminals: RL = Rth.
Proof. Replace the network by its Thevenin equivalent Vth in series with Rth, connected to a variable load RL.
Step 1: Load current I = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>).
Step 2: Power in load P = I²R<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>² R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)².

Step 3: For maximum P, dP/dR<sub>L</sub> = 0: dP/dR<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>² [ (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)² − 2R<sub>L</sub>(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>) ] / (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)<sup>4</sup> = 0.
Step 4: (Rth + RL) − 2RL = 0, so Rth − RL = 0, i.e. RL = Rth.

Step 5: The second derivative at R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> is negative (= −V<sub>th</sub>²/8R<sub>th</sub>³), so the power is a maximum. P is zero at R<sub>L</sub> = 0 and R<sub>L</sub> = ∞ and peaks in between.
Step 6: Substituting RL = Rth: Pmax = Vth² Rth/(2Rth)² = Vth²/4Rth.

Efficiency. Power delivered to load = I²RL; power generated by the source = I²(Rth + RL). η = RL/(Rth + RL) × 100. At RL = Rth, η = Rth/2Rth = 50 %. Half of the power is lost in the source resistance. Hence maximum power transfer is used in communication/low-power circuits where power level is small; power systems operate at high efficiency with RL much greater than the source resistance.
formulas: η = R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>L</sub> + R<sub>th</sub>) = 50 % at max power

answer: Principle. A star (Y) network of RA, RB, RC and a delta (Δ) network of RAB, RBC, RCA are equivalent when the resistance measured between every pair of terminals A–B, B–C, C–A is the same in both, with the third terminal open.
Delta, between A and B: RAB ∥ (RBC + RCA) = RAB(RBC + RCA)/(RAB + RBC + RCA). Let RΔ = RAB + RBC + RCA.
Star, between A and B: RA + RB.

Equating: (1) R<sub>A</sub> + R<sub>B</sub> = R<sub>AB</sub>(R<sub>BC</sub> + R<sub>CA</sub>)/R<sub>Δ</sub>. Similarly (2) R<sub>B</sub> + R<sub>C</sub> = R<sub>BC</sub>(R<sub>CA</sub> + R<sub>AB</sub>)/R<sub>Δ</sub> and (3) R<sub>C</sub> + R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>CA</sub>(R<sub>AB</sub> + R<sub>BC</sub>)/R<sub>Δ</sub>.

Delta → Star. Add (1) and (3) and subtract (2): 2RA = [RABRBC + RABRCA + RCARAB + RCARBC − RBCRCA − RBCRAB]/RΔ = 2RABRCA/RΔ. Hence RA = RABRCA/(RAB + RBC + RCA); likewise RB = RABRBC/RΔ and RC = RBCRCA/RΔ. (Rule: product of the two delta resistors adjacent to the terminal ÷ sum of all three.)

Star → Delta. Form RARB + RBRC + RCRA = RABRBCRCA(RAB + RBC + RCA)/RΔ² = RABRBCRCA/RΔ. Divide by RC = RBCRCA/RΔ: (RARB + RBRC + RCRA)/RC = RAB. Hence RAB = RA + RB + RARB/RC, and cyclically RBC = RB + RC + RBRC/RA, RCA = RC + RA + RCRA/RB.
Balanced case. If RA = RB = RC = RY, then RΔ = 3RY; conversely RY = RΔ/3. These transformations simplify bridge networks that are neither series nor parallel.

answer: First-order circuit. A circuit containing resistors and only one energy-storage element (one L or one C) is a first-order circuit; its response is described by a first-order linear differential equation, and the transient is a single exponential.

DC steady state. After the transient dies out, currents and voltages are constant, so di/dt = 0 and dv/dt = 0. Hence vL = L di/dt = 0: an inductor behaves as a short circuit. iC = C dv/dt = 0: a capacitor behaves as an open circuit (and is charged to the source voltage).
Series R-L, DC V applied at t = 0 (i(0) = 0). KVL: V = iR + L di/dt.
Rearranging: di/(V − iR) = dt/L. Integrate: −(1/R) ln(V − iR) = t/L + K. At t = 0, i = 0 gives K = −(1/R) ln V.
So ln[(V − iR)/V] = −Rt/L, thus i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e−t/τ), τ = L/R. Also vL = L di/dt = V e−t/τ, vR = V(1 − e−t/τ). The current rises from 0 to the final value V/R.
Series R-C, DC V applied at t = 0 (vC(0) = 0). KVL: V = iR + vC, with i = C dvC/dt, so RC dvC/dt + vC = V.
Separate variables: dvC/(V − vC) = dt/RC. Integrate: −ln(V − vC) = t/RC + K; at t = 0, vC = 0 gives K = −ln V. Hence vC(t) = V(1 − e−t/τ), τ = RC, and i(t) = (V/R)e−t/τ.

Time constant τ. It is the time in which the quantity reaches 63.2 % of its final value during rise (or falls to 36.8 % of its initial value during decay); the tangent at t = 0 meets the final value at t = τ. After 5τ the response is within 1 % of the final value, i.e. the transient is considered over. Larger τ means slower response. For discharge (source removed): i = (V/R)e−t/τ in RL and vC = V e−t/τ in RC.
formulas: R-C: v<sub>C</sub>(t) = V(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>), τ = RC

answer: Definitions. (i) Instantaneous value – the value of the alternating quantity at any particular instant, e.g. i = Im sin ωt. (ii) Peak (maximum) value Im – the largest value reached in a half cycle (amplitude). (iii) Average value – the mean of all instantaneous values over a half cycle (the full-cycle mean of a sine wave is zero). (iv) RMS (effective) value – the square root of the mean of the squares of the instantaneous values over a cycle; it equals the DC value that produces the same heating effect in a resistor. (v) Form factor Kf = RMS value / average value. (vi) Peak (crest) factor Kp = peak value / RMS value.
Waveform. Let i = Im sin θ, where θ = ωt, one cycle being 0 to 2π (draw a sine wave with positive and negative half-cycles, marking Im and the period T).
Derivation of RMS value. By definition Irms = √[ (1/2π) ∫02π i² dθ ].
Step 1: i² = I<sub>m</sub>² sin²θ = I<sub>m</sub>² (1 − cos 2θ)/2.
Step 2: ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> i² dθ = (I<sub>m</sub>²/2) [θ − (sin 2θ)/2]<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> = (I<sub>m</sub>²/2)(2π) = π I<sub>m</sub>².
Step 3: Irms = √[ (1/2π)(π Im²) ] = √(Im²/2) = Im/√2 = 0.707 Im.
Derivation of average value. Taken over the half cycle 0 to π (the full cycle gives zero because the two halves cancel): Iav = (1/π) ∫0π Im sin θ dθ.
Step 4: Iav = (Im/π) [−cos θ]0π = (Im/π)(1 + 1) = 2Im/π = 0.637 Im.
Form factor Kf = Irms/Iav = 0.707 Im/0.637 Im = 1.11.
Peak factor Kp = Im/Irms = Im/0.707 Im = 1.414.
Significance: a.c. meters are calibrated in RMS values; the 230 V domestic supply is the RMS value, its peak being 230√2 ≈ 325 V.

answer: (a) Active (true) power P. The power actually converted to useful work or heat in the circuit: P = VI cosφ = I²R, unit watt (W).
Reactive power Q. The power exchanged back and forth between the source and the L and C elements, doing no net work: Q = VI sinφ = I²X, unit volt-ampere reactive (VAR).
Apparent power S. The product of RMS voltage and RMS current, S = VI, unit volt-ampere (VA). S = √(P² + Q²).
Power factor. cosφ = P/S = R/Z = cosine of the angle between V and I; it is lagging for inductive loads and leading for capacitive loads (0 ≤ cosφ ≤ 1).
Power triangle. Right-angled triangle with base P (W), perpendicular Q (VAR) and hypotenuse S (VA), angle φ between S and P: P = S cosφ, Q = S sinφ, tanφ = Q/P.

(b) Causes of low power factor. (i) Induction motors and transformers lightly loaded (large magnetising current). (ii) Fluorescent/discharge lamps with chokes. (iii) Arc and induction furnaces, welding sets. (iv) Varying load on the supply and highly inductive loads in industry.

Disadvantages. For a given power P and voltage V, I = P/(V cosφ), so a low cosφ means: (i) larger current and hence larger I²R losses in lines and transformers; (ii) larger cable/conductor size and higher capital cost; (iii) larger kVA rating of generators and transformers for the same kW; (iv) poor voltage regulation due to larger voltage drop; (v) lower efficiency and penalty (low-p.f. surcharge) in tariff.

Improvement by shunt capacitor bank. A capacitor connected in parallel with the inductive load draws a leading current IC = V/XC which cancels part of the lagging reactive component of the load current; the real component is unchanged so the supply current falls and the angle reduces from φ1 to φ2.
Phasor diagram: V reference; load current I<sub>1</sub> lags by φ<sub>1</sub>; I<sub>C</sub> leads V by 90°; resultant I lags by smaller φ<sub>2</sub>.

Capacitor required: reactive power supplied QC = P(tanφ1 − tanφ2) = V²/XC = ωCV², hence C = P(tanφ1 − tanφ2)/(ωV²) (single phase). Capacitor banks are used at the load end or at substations, and synchronous condensers are an alternative.

answer: Resonance. A series R-L-C circuit is said to be in resonance when the supply voltage and the current are in phase, i.e. the circuit behaves as a pure resistance (power factor unity). This occurs when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance.
Condition and resonant frequency. Impedance Z = √[R² + (XL − XC)²]. Phase angle φ = tan⁻¹[(XL − XC)/R] = 0 requires XL = XC.
At resonance ω0L = 1/(ω0C) ⇒ ω0² = 1/LC ⇒ ω0 = 1/√(LC) rad/s, hence f0 = 1/(2π√LC).
Characteristics at resonance. Z = R (minimum); I0 = V/R (maximum); p.f. = 1; VL = VC (equal and opposite, cancelling), VR = V; the circuit is purely resistive.

Variation with frequency (sketch). XL = 2πfL is a straight line through the origin; XC = 1/2πfC is a rectangular hyperbola falling with f; they cross at f0. R is a horizontal line. Z = √[R² + (XL − XC)²] is a U-shaped curve with minimum R at f0; I = V/Z is a bell-shaped curve with maximum V/R at f0. Below f0 the circuit is capacitive (current leads), above f0 inductive (current lags).

Half-power frequencies and bandwidth. The frequencies f1 and f2 at which the current falls to I0/√2 (power falls to half of its maximum) are the half-power points. Bandwidth Δf = f2 − f1 = R/2πL = f0/Q.
Quality factor. Q = (voltage across L or C at resonance)/(supply voltage) = ω0L/R = 1/(ω0CR) = (1/R)√(L/C). It measures the sharpness of resonance (selectivity); high Q means narrow bandwidth.

Voltage magnification. At resonance I0 = V/R, so VL = I0XL = (V/R)ω0L = QV and VC = I0XC = QV. Since Q is usually much greater than 1, the voltages across L and C can be many times the supply voltage (hence the name voltage resonance), although they are in antiphase and cancel in the total. Application: tuning circuits in radio receivers.

A. Star (Y) connection. The similar ends of the three phases are joined to form the neutral N; the other ends R, Y, B go to the lines. The line current flows through exactly one phase, so IL = Iph.

Take V<sub>RN</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠0°, V<sub>YN</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠−120°, V<sub>BN</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠−240°. The line voltage is the potential difference between two lines: V<sub>RY</sub> = V<sub>RN</sub> − V<sub>YN</sub> (phasor difference).

Phasor diagram: draw V<sub>RN</sub> and reverse V<sub>YN</sub> (−V<sub>YN</sub>); the angle between V<sub>RN</sub> and −V<sub>YN</sub> is 60°. Then V<sub>RY</sub>² = V<sub>ph</sub>² + V<sub>ph</sub>² + 2V<sub>ph</sub>² cos 60° = 3V<sub>ph</sub>².
Hence VL = √3 Vph, and VRY leads VRN by 30°. Similarly for VYB and VBR.

B. Delta (Δ) connection. The end of each phase is joined to the start of the next to form a closed mesh; the lines are taken from the three junctions. Each phase is directly across two lines, so VL = Vph.

Phase currents I<sub>RY</sub>, I<sub>YB</sub>, I<sub>BR</sub> (each I<sub>ph</sub>) are 120° apart. Applying KCL at a junction, the line current I<sub>R</sub> = I<sub>RY</sub> − I<sub>BR</sub> (phasor difference).

Hence IL = √3 Iph, and IR lags IRY by 30°.
Power. In both connections P = 3VphIphcosφ = √3 VLIL cosφ, where φ is the angle between phase voltage and phase current.

answer: Principle. For a 3-wire, 3-phase system (balanced or unbalanced, star or delta) the total instantaneous power is p = vRiR + vYiY + vBiB with iR + iY + iB = 0. Eliminating iB gives p = (vR − vB) iR + (vY − vB) iY. Hence two wattmeters suffice, and total power P = W1 + W2.

Connections. The current coil of W1 is in line R and that of W2 in line Y; the pressure coils of both are connected between their own line (R and Y respectively) and the third line B. W1 reads VRB IR cos(angle between them); W2 reads VYB IY cos(angle). The same connection applies to a balanced star load and a balanced delta load (the load itself is any 3-wire balanced load).

Phasor diagram (inductive load). Draw the phase voltages VR, VY, VB at 120°; the phase currents IR, IY, IB lag their phase voltages by φ. VRB = VR − VB leads VR by 30° and VYB = VY − VB lags VY by 30°, each of magnitude VL.
Angle between V<sub>RB</sub> and I<sub>R</sub> = 30° − φ; angle between V<sub>YB</sub> and I<sub>Y</sub> = 30° + φ.
So W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° − φ) and W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° + φ).
Sum: W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>[cos(30° − φ) + cos(30° + φ)] = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> · 2 cos30° cosφ = √3 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cosφ = total power ✓.
Difference: W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>[cos(30° − φ) − cos(30° + φ)] = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> · 2 sin30° sinφ = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> sinφ.
Dividing: (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2) = sinφ/(√3 cosφ), hence tanφ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2), from which the power factor cosφ is found.
Discussion. (i) p.f. = 1 (φ = 0): W1 = W2 = VLIL cos30°; both read equal and positive.

(ii) p.f. = 0.5 (φ = 60°): W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos90° = 0 and W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos30°; one wattmeter reads zero and the other reads the whole power. For p.f. < 0.5 (φ > 60°) W<sub>2</sub> becomes negative and its connections must be reversed.

(iii) p.f. = 0 (φ = 90°): W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(−60°) = +½V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> and W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos120° = −½V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>; equal and opposite readings, total power zero.

answer: Similarities. Both circuits have a driving force, a flow quantity and an opposition obeying a form of Ohm's law: Electric: EMF (V) – current I – resistance R = ρl/A – conductance G = 1/R – current density J = I/A – I = EMF/R. Magnetic: MMF (AT) – flux Φ – reluctance S = l/(μ0μrA) – permeance 1/S – flux density B = Φ/A – Φ = MMF/S. Series and parallel laws are alike (Stotal = S1 + S2 in series; 1/S = 1/S1 + 1/S2 in parallel), and Kirchhoff-type laws hold (ΣΦ = 0 at a junction, ΣNI = ΣΦS around a loop).

Dissimilarities. (i) Current actually flows (charge motion) whereas flux does not 'flow'; it is only established. (ii) Energy is continuously dissipated (I²R) in an electric circuit while no energy is needed to maintain constant flux (only to set it up). (iii) Resistance is practically constant but reluctance varies with flux density (saturation, μr not constant). (iv) Conductors can be insulated perfectly, but there is no insulator for flux – leakage and fringing always exist. (v) Resistivity is temperature dependent, permeability is not significantly.

Faraday's laws. First law: whenever the flux linked with a coil changes, an EMF is induced in it. Second law: the magnitude of the induced EMF equals the rate of change of flux linkages, e = −N dΦ/dt (volts).
Lenz's law. The direction of the induced EMF (and current) is such that it opposes the cause producing it – this is the origin of the minus sign.

Definitions. MMF (magnetomotive force) = NI ampere-turns, the cause producing flux. Reluctance S = MMF/Φ = l/(μA), unit AT/Wb (or H⁻¹): the opposition to establishment of flux. Permeance = 1/S, unit Wb/AT (henry). Flux density B = Φ/A, unit tesla (Wb/m²); B = μH.

Electrical dual of a parallel-limb (composite) magnetic circuit. Centre limb of reluctance S carries the total flux Φ and side limbs of reluctances S1 and S2 carry Φ1 and Φ2 in parallel, with Φ = Φ1 + Φ2. The MMF source NI (analogue of a battery) is in series with S; S1 and S2 are in parallel across the source branch. Equivalent: Seq = S + S1S2/(S1 + S2), Φ = NI/Seq.

answer: Principle. A single-phase transformer is a static device which transfers electrical energy from one a.c. circuit to another at the same frequency, by mutual induction (Faraday's law). When an alternating voltage is applied to the primary, an alternating flux is set up in the core, which links the secondary and induces an EMF in it.

Construction. (i) Magnetic core of laminated sheets of silicon steel (0.35–0.5 mm, insulated by varnish) to reduce eddy-current and hysteresis loss. (ii) Two separate windings, primary (N1 turns) and secondary (N2 turns), of insulated copper, electrically isolated but magnetically coupled. (iii) Tank with transformer oil (for large units) for cooling and insulation, bushings, conservator.

Core type: the windings surround the core; two limbs and two yokes form a single rectangular magnetic path; primary on one limb and secondary on the other (or both split concentrically over each limb, LV next to core). Shell type: three-limbed core with both windings on the central limb; the flux of the central limb divides equally into the two outer limbs, providing a double magnetic path. Core type is used for high-voltage, shell type for low-voltage and low power.

Working. The primary current produces alternating flux Φ in the core. By Faraday's law this flux induces E1 (opposing V1, self-induction) in the primary and E2 in the secondary. With a load connected, secondary current flows and power is delivered at the same frequency.
EMF equation. Let N1 = primary turns, f = frequency, Φm = maximum flux (Wb). Flux varies sinusoidally: Φ = Φm sin ωt.
Step 1: Instantaneous induced EMF e<sub>1</sub> = −N<sub>1</sub> dΦ/dt = −N<sub>1</sub>ωΦ<sub>m</sub> cos ωt = N<sub>1</sub>ωΦ<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt − 90°).
Step 2: Maximum value E<sub>m</sub> = N<sub>1</sub>ωΦ<sub>m</sub> = 2πf N<sub>1</sub> Φ<sub>m</sub>.
Step 3: RMS value E1 = Em/√2 = (2π/√2) f N1 Φm = 4.44 f N1 Φm. Hence E1 = 4.44 f N1 Φm volts, and similarly E2 = 4.44 f N2 Φm.

Step 4: Dividing, E<sub>2</sub>/E<sub>1</sub> = N<sub>2</sub>/N<sub>1</sub> = K (transformation ratio). Induced EMF lags the flux by 90°. Also Φ<sub>m</sub> = B<sub>m</sub>A<sub>i</sub> for core area A<sub>i</sub>.

rubric.point: Ideal transformer definition and characteristics (no resistance, no leakage, no losses, infinite μ, 100% efficiency)
Practical transformer differences (winding resistance, leakage flux, core loss, magnetising current)
Basic relations V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub> = N<sub>1</sub>/N<sub>2</sub> = I<sub>2</sub>/I<sub>1</sub>
Phasor diagram at unity p.f. with all quantities labelled
Phasor diagram at lagging p.f.

Expressions for E<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>2</sub> with drops (V<sub>1</sub> = E<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>1</sub>(R<sub>1</sub> + jX<sub>1</sub>), E<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub>(R<sub>2</sub> + jX<sub>2</sub>))

answer: Ideal transformer. One with (i) zero winding resistance, (ii) no leakage flux (coefficient of coupling = 1), (iii) no core loss (hysteresis and eddy), (iv) infinitely permeable core needing negligible magnetising current, (v) hence 100% efficiency and zero voltage regulation. Then V1/V2 = E1/E2 = N1/N2 = I2/I1 and V1I1 = V2I2. Magnetising current and core-loss current are zero, and primary and secondary mmfs balance exactly (N1I1 = N2I2).

Practical transformer. Windings have resistance R1, R2 (copper loss); some flux leaks and produces leakage reactances X1, X2; the core has finite permeability, so a no-load current I0 = Ic + Im (Ic in phase with E1 for iron loss, Im lagging 90° to magnetise) is drawn; efficiency is less than 100% and there is voltage drop on load.
Basic equations (load). Secondary: E2 = V2 + I2(R2 + jX2). Primary: V1 = E1 + I1(R1 + jX1) with E1 = 4.44 f N1 Φm, I1 = I0 + I2' where I2' = (N2/N1) I2.

Phasor diagram – unity p.f. load. Step 1: take main flux Φ as reference. Step 2: E1 and E2 lag Φ by 90° (−E1 is drawn 180° opposite, equal to V1 balance). Step 3: V2 is drawn along I2 (φ2 = 0). Step 4: add I2R2 parallel to I2 and I2X2 perpendicular (leading by 90°) to V2 to get E2. Step 5: draw I0 (Im along Φ, Ic along −E1), add I2' = −(N2/N1)I2 to get I1. Step 6: V1 = −E1 + I1R1 + jI1X1; angle between V1 and I1 is φ1, slightly more than zero.

Phasor diagram – lagging p.f. (R-L load). The same construction is used, but I2 lags V2 by φ2; the I2R2 drop is drawn parallel to I2 and I2X2 perpendicular to it, so E2 is larger than V2 and the arithmetic difference E2 − V2 ≈ I2(R2 cosφ2 + X2 sinφ2) is greatest. I1 lags V1 by φ1, and the no-load current I0 is seen to be a small part of I1.

Terminal voltages. V2 = E2 − I2(R2 + jX2) and V1 = −E1 + I1(R1 + jX1). Hence a lagging load gives a fall in secondary terminal voltage on load; a leading p.f. load can even raise V2 (Ferranti-like effect).

rubric.point: Classification of losses: iron (hysteresis, eddy current) and copper losses
Minimising hysteresis loss (silicon steel, CRGO) and eddy loss (lamination)
Efficiency expression η = x S cosφ/(x S cosφ + P<sub>i</sub> + x²P<sub>cu</sub>)
Differentiation dη/dx = 0 / minimising losses
Condition P<sub>i</sub> = x²P<sub>cu</sub> (iron loss = copper loss)
Load at maximum efficiency x = √(P<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>cu</sub>), I<sub>2</sub> = I<sub>FL</sub>√(P<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>cu</sub>) and η<sub>max</sub>

answer: Losses in a transformer. (A) Core (iron) losses – constant at constant V and f: (i) hysteresis loss Ph = kh Bm1.6 f V; (ii) eddy-current loss Pe = ke Bm² f² t² V. (B) Copper losses – I1²R1 + I2²R2 = I²Re, varying with the square of the load current. (C) Stray/dielectric losses (small). There are no rotational losses, hence high efficiency (95–99%).
Minimising hysteresis loss. Use core material with a narrow B–H loop (small area) – silicon steel (3–4% Si) or cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) steel, which has low coercivity and high permeability.

Minimising eddy-current loss. Build the core from thin laminations (0.35–0.5 mm) insulated from each other by varnish/oxide; since Pe ∝ t², thin laminations break up the eddy paths and raise the resistance; silicon also increases resistivity of the steel.

Condition for maximum efficiency. Let x be the fraction of full load, S the rated kVA, cosφ the load p.f., Pi the iron loss and Pcu the full-load copper loss. Output = x S cosφ; copper loss at load x = x²Pcu.
Step 1: η = x S cosφ/(x S cosφ + P<sub>i</sub> + x²P<sub>cu</sub>).

Step 2: For fixed V, f and cosφ, η is maximum when the denominator per unit output is minimum: d/dx [ (x S cosφ + P<sub>i</sub> + x²P<sub>cu</sub>)/(x S cosφ) ] = 0, i.e. d/dx [ 1 + P<sub>i</sub>/(x S cosφ) + x P<sub>cu</sub>/(S cosφ) ] = 0.
Step 3: −P<sub>i</sub>/(x² S cosφ) + P<sub>cu</sub>/(S cosφ) = 0 ⇒ P<sub>i</sub> = x² P<sub>cu</sub>.

Hence efficiency is maximum when the variable (copper) loss equals the constant (iron) loss. The second derivative is positive, confirming a maximum (efficiency is independent of p.f. as the condition).

Step 4: Fraction of full load at maximum efficiency x = √(P<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>cu</sub>). Load current at maximum efficiency I<sub>2</sub> = x I<sub>2,FL</sub> = I<sub>2,FL</sub> √(P<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>cu</sub>). Corresponding kVA = S√(P<sub>i</sub>/P<sub>cu</sub>).

Step 5: η<sub>max</sub> = x S cosφ/(x S cosφ + 2P<sub>i</sub>). Also, in terms of equivalent resistance, I<sub>2</sub> at η<sub>max</sub> satisfies I<sub>2</sub>²R<sub>2e</sub> = P<sub>i</sub> ⇒ I<sub>2</sub> = √(P<sub>i</sub>/R<sub>2e</sub>).
formulas: η = x S cosφ/(x S cosφ + P<sub>i</sub> + x²P<sub>cu</sub>)
η<sub>max</sub> = x S cosφ/(x S cosφ + 2P<sub>i</sub>)

rubric.point: Principle/construction of autotransformer (single common winding) with diagram
Comparison of copper saving: factor (1 − K) and conductor weight
Efficiency, size, regulation and reactance comparison
Electrical isolation lacking in autotransformer vs isolation in two-winding
Applications of both

answer: Two-winding transformer. Primary and secondary are separate windings, magnetically coupled but electrically isolated; power is transferred entirely by transformer action (induction).

Autotransformer. A transformer with a single continuous winding, part of which is common to the primary and the secondary (tapped at a point). Power is transferred partly by conduction (direct electrical connection) and partly by induction. With K = N2/N1 (<1 step-down), input VA = V1I1 of which a fraction K is conducted directly and (1 − K) is transferred by induction.

Copper saving. Weight of copper in autotransformer = (1 − K) × weight in a two-winding transformer of the same rating (K < 1). For K = 0.8, 20% copper is saved; saving is greatest when K is close to 1. Core and size are also smaller.

(i) Copper/size/cost: less in autotransformer. (ii) Efficiency: higher in autotransformer (less copper loss, smaller leakage) for the same kVA. (iii) Voltage regulation: better (lower leakage reactance and resistance). (iv) Isolation: two-winding gives complete electrical isolation between primary and secondary; autotransformer gives none, so a fault on the HV side can put full voltage on the LV side – hazardous for safety. (v) Short-circuit currents are larger in autotransformers because of low impedance. (vi) Economical only when K is near 1 (ratio up to about 2).

Applications. Autotransformer: starting of induction and synchronous motors, variable-voltage supply (variac), voltage boosting/buck in distribution, interconnecting grids of similar voltages (e.g. 220/132 kV). Two-winding: isolation transformers, distribution transformers, large step-up/step-down ratios, instrument and welding transformers.
formulas: Cu saving = K × (weight of Cu in two-winding)

rubric.point: Classification of instruments (absolute/secondary; indicating, recording, integrating; analogue/digital)
Deflecting torque with examples of effects used
Controlling torque (spring/gravity) and equilibrium θ relation
Damping torque (air friction, fluid, eddy-current) and critical damping
PMMC construction with labelled diagram
PMMC torque equation T<sub>d</sub> = NBAI and θ = (NBA/K)I (linear scale)
Why PMMC works only on DC
Advantages and disadvantages of PMMC

answer: Classification. (A) Absolute instruments (tangent galvanometer) give the quantity from instrument constants; secondary instruments are calibrated against absolute ones and are of three kinds: (i) indicating (ammeter, voltmeter, wattmeter), (ii) integrating (energy meter), (iii) recording (recorders). By working principle: moving-coil (PMMC, dynamometer), moving-iron, induction, electrostatic, thermal, rectifier types. By display: analogue and digital.

Torques required in an indicating instrument. (i) Deflecting torque Td – produced by the electrical quantity (magnetic, heating, electrostatic or induction effect) and moves the pointer from zero. (ii) Controlling torque Tc – opposes Td, provided by a hair spring (Tc = Kθ) or gravity, so that the deflection is a definite measure of the quantity; it also returns the pointer to zero. At steady deflection Td = Tc. (iii) Damping torque Tv – proportional to angular velocity, stops oscillation about the final position so that the pointer settles quickly (critical damping); provided by air friction (piston/vane), fluid friction or eddy-current damping.

PMMC construction. A rectangular coil of N turns (aluminium former) pivoted on jewelled bearings between the poles of a strong permanent horseshoe magnet with soft-iron pole pieces and a fixed cylindrical soft-iron core which produces a uniform radial field B in the air gap. Current is led in and out through two spiral hair springs, which also give the controlling torque; the pointer, balance weights and scale complete the instrument. Damping is by eddy currents induced in the aluminium former.

Principle and torque equation. A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a force (F = BIl) producing a torque. Each side of length l carries force BIlN; with width b, deflecting torque Td = N B I l b = N B A I (A = lb). Controlling torque Tc = Kθ. In equilibrium NBAI = Kθ ⇒ θ = (NBA/K) I ∝ I.
Because θ ∝ I (B constant by radial uniform field and K constant), the scale is uniform (linear).

DC only. The torque direction depends on the current direction. On a.c., the torque reverses every half cycle; the moving system cannot follow the frequency, so the average torque is zero and the pointer only vibrates about zero. Hence PMMC measures DC only (with a rectifier it can read a.c.).

Advantages: uniform scale, high sensitivity and accuracy, low power consumption, effective eddy-current damping, unaffected by stray fields. Disadvantages: DC only, costlier, ageing of magnet and springs, overload can burn springs/coil.

rubric.point: Construction of DC machine with labelled parts (yoke, poles, armature, commutator, brushes)
Operating principle of DC generator (Faraday's law, Fleming's right-hand rule)
Derivation of EMF equation E<sub>g</sub> = PΦZN/60A with steps
Working principle of DC motor (force on conductor, Fleming's left-hand rule, torque)
Back EMF E<sub>b</sub> = V − I<sub>a</sub>R<sub>a</sub>
Significance of back EMF: self-regulation of armature current and power conversion

answer: Construction. (i) Yoke – cast iron/steel frame, mechanical support and path for flux. (ii) Field poles with pole shoes and field winding – produce the main flux. (iii) Armature – laminated core with slots carrying armature conductors (lap or wave wound). (iv) Commutator – hard-drawn copper segments insulated by mica; converts the alternating armature EMF into unidirectional output. (v) Brushes (carbon) with brush gear collecting current; (vi) bearings and shaft.

Principle of generator. Whenever a conductor cuts magnetic flux, an EMF is induced in it (Faraday's law); its direction is given by Fleming's right-hand rule. The armature conductors rotating in the field of the poles develop an alternating EMF, which the commutator rectifies to DC at the brushes.
EMF equation. Let Φ = flux per pole (Wb), P = number of poles, Z = total armature conductors, A = number of parallel paths (A = P lap, A = 2 wave), N = speed in rpm.
Step 1: Flux cut by one conductor in one revolution = PΦ Wb. Time of one revolution = 60/N s.
Step 2: Average EMF induced per conductor e = PΦ/(60/N) = PΦN/60 volts.
Step 3: Number of conductors in series per parallel path = Z/A. The EMF of the generator equals that of one path:
Eg = (PΦN/60) × (Z/A) = PΦZN/(60A) volts. For a given machine Eg = KΦN where K = PZ/60A; in terms of ω: Eg = (PZ/2πA) Φ ω.

DC motor – principle. A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force F = BIl (Fleming's left-hand rule). The forces on the conductors under the N and S poles produce a torque T = KΦIa which rotates the armature. The commutator reverses the current in a conductor as it passes the neutral axis, so that the torque keeps the same direction.

Back EMF. The armature conductors of the motor rotate in the field and cut flux, so an EMF Eb = PΦZN/60A is induced that opposes the applied voltage (Lenz's law). Voltage equation: V = Eb + IaRa ⇒ Ia = (V − Eb)/Ra.

Significance. (i) Eb acts as a governor: if the load increases, the speed falls, Eb falls, Ia rises and the torque increases to meet the load; if the load decreases, the reverse occurs – the motor automatically draws just the current the load needs. (ii) At start N = 0, Eb = 0, so Ia = V/Ra is dangerously large; hence a starter is needed. (iii) Electrical power input VIa is converted to mechanical power: Pm = EbIa, i.e. Eb represents the energy conversion; gross mechanical power is maximum when Eb = V/2.

T ∝ ΦIa and Φ is constant, so the torque–current characteristic (T versus Ia) is a straight line through the origin. Speed N = (V − IaRa)/KΦ, so the speed–torque curve is a slightly drooping straight line (a 3–5% fall from no-load to full load): the motor is an almost constant speed motor. Armature reaction slightly lowers Φ and reduces the droop.
Sketch: T–I<sub>a</sub> straight line passing through the origin; N–T line falling slightly from no-load speed N<sub>0</sub> = V/KΦ with torque.

Speed control. From N ∝ (V − IaRa)/Φ the speed can be varied by: (i) Armature resistance control – a variable resistance Re in series with the armature lowers the voltage to the armature, so speed is reduced below normal; simple, but wasteful (I²R loss) and gives poor speed regulation. (ii) Armature voltage control – varying V applied to the armature (Ward-Leonard or thyristor converter) gives smooth speed variation from zero up to base speed at constant torque, with good regulation and high efficiency.

(iii) Field flux weakening – a rheostat in the field circuit reduces If and hence Φ; N ∝ 1/Φ increases above base speed (constant power region), limited by commutation and mechanical stress; torque per ampere falls since T ∝ Φ.

Need for a starter. At the instant of starting, N = 0 and Eb = 0, so Ia = V/Ra, which may be 20–30 times the rated current because Ra is very small; this would burn the armature, damage the commutator and cause a heavy line-voltage dip. A starter inserts an external resistance in series with the armature, reducing it step by step as the back EMF builds up.

Three-point starter. Parts: a rheostat with contact studs, resistance steps, a hinged spring-loaded handle (start arm), a soft-iron piece that is held by the no-volt coil (NVC, hold-on coil) in series with the shunt field, and an overload release (OLR, electromagnet) with a short-circuiting strip. The three terminals are L (line), A (armature) and F (field).

Working. Handle moved from OFF to the first stud: the full resistance is in series with the armature while the field gets full supply through the NVC. As the motor speeds up, the handle is moved slowly over successive studs to cut out resistance; at the last stud the iron piece is held by the NVC against the spring force, with no resistance in the armature. NVC: if supply fails or the field current is too low, the NVC releases the handle and the spring returns it to OFF – protection against no-voltage restart and field failure (the motor would race). OLR: on overload the magnet attracts its armature, lifting it to short-circuit the NVC, which releases the handle – protecting against excess current.

rubric.point: Definition of rotating magnetic field with spatial arrangement (windings 120° apart)
Statement of three-phase currents and fluxes as functions of time
Resolution of fluxes into horizontal and vertical components
Resultant flux of constant magnitude 1.5Φ<sub>m</sub>
Proof of rotation at angular speed ω and N<sub>s</sub> = 120f/P
Reversal of direction by interchanging two supply leads

answer: Rotating magnetic field. A magnetic field of constant magnitude whose axis rotates in space at constant angular speed. It is produced by a balanced 3-phase winding (three coils displaced 120° in space) carrying balanced 3-phase currents.

Fluxes. Phase currents: iR = Im sin ωt, iY = Im sin(ωt − 120°), iB = Im sin(ωt − 240°). Each current produces a pulsating flux along its own coil axis: ΦR = Φm sin ωt (axis at 0°), ΦY = Φm sin(ωt − 120°) (axis at 120°), ΦB = Φm sin(ωt − 240°) (axis at 240°).

Resultant – horizontal component. Φx = ΦR + ΦY cos120° + ΦB cos240° = Φm[sin ωt − ½ sin(ωt − 120°) − ½ sin(ωt − 240°)]. Since sin(ωt − 120°) + sin(ωt − 240°) = 2 sin(ωt − 180°) cos60° = − sin ωt, Φx = Φm[sin ωt + ½ sin ωt] = 1.5 Φm sin ωt.
Vertical component. Φy = ΦY sin120° + ΦB sin240° = (√3/2)Φm[sin(ωt − 120°) − sin(ωt − 240°)] = (√3/2)Φm · 2cos(ωt − 180°) sin60° = (√3/2)Φm(−√3 cos ωt) = −1.5 Φm cos ωt.
Resultant magnitude. Φr = √(Φx² + Φy²) = 1.5Φm √(sin²ωt + cos²ωt) = 1.5 Φm, a constant, independent of time.

Direction. tan θ = Φy/Φx = −cot ωt = tan(ωt − 90°), so θ = ωt − 90°. The axis of the resultant flux therefore rotates with angular velocity dθ/dt = ω = 2πf rad/s, i.e. one revolution per cycle for a 2-pole winding. (Check: at ωt = 0, ΦR = 0, ΦY = −0.866Φm, ΦB = +0.866Φm; resultant 1.5Φm at −90°; at ωt = 60° it has moved 60°.)
Synchronous speed. For a P-pole winding the field moves through one pole pair per cycle, so Ns = 120 f/P rpm.

Reversal. The direction of rotation depends on the phase sequence (R-Y-B). Interchanging any two of the three supply lines to the stator (reversing the phase sequence) reverses the direction of the RMF and hence the motor.

rubric.point: Construction of 3-phase induction motor: stator, rotor, air gap with diagram
Working principle: RMF, induced rotor EMF, Lenz's law, torque
Why asynchronous, why rotor cannot reach N<sub>s</sub>; slip s = (N<sub>s</sub> − N)/N<sub>s</sub>
Squirrel-cage rotor construction and features
Slip-ring (wound) rotor construction, external resistance and features
Torque–slip characteristic with motoring, generating and braking regions and key points (starting torque, T<sub>max</sub>)

answer: Construction. Stator: laminated silicon steel frame with slots carrying a 3-phase winding for P poles. Rotor: laminated cylindrical core on the shaft with slots for rotor conductors. A small air gap (0.3–1 mm) separates them. Stator is connected to the supply; no electrical connection feeds the rotor.

Working principle. The stator current sets up an RMF of speed Ns = 120f/P which cuts the stationary rotor conductors, inducing EMF in them (Faraday's law). The rotor circuit is closed, so rotor currents flow. By Lenz's law, the rotor tries to oppose the cause (relative speed between field and rotor), so a torque (force on current-carrying conductors in the field) drags the rotor in the direction of the RMF.

Asynchronous. The rotor speed N is always less than Ns. If N = Ns, the relative speed between field and conductors would be zero, no EMF or current would be induced and no torque would be produced; friction would slow the rotor. Hence the motor runs at N < Ns; the difference is the slip: s = (Ns − N)/Ns, typically 2–5% at full load. The rotor-frequency fr = sf.

Squirrel-cage rotor. Slots contain uninsulated copper/aluminium bars short-circuited at both ends by end rings (like a cage); bars are skewed to reduce noise and cogging. Simple, rugged, cheap, maintenance free, higher efficiency; no external resistance can be added, so starting torque is low (1.5–2 × full load torque) with high starting current.

Phase-wound (slip-ring) rotor. Rotor carries a 3-phase star-connected winding (same poles as stator), the three ends being brought out to three slip rings with brushes connected to an external 3-phase rheostat. External resistance gives high starting torque with low starting current, then it is cut out; it also allows speed control. More expensive, needs maintenance.

Torque–slip characteristic. T = k s E₂²R₂/(R₂² + s²X₂²) (rotor quantities at standstill). For s from 1 to 0 (motoring region, 0 < s ≤ 1): T = starting torque at s = 1, rises to maximum (breakdown) torque Tmax at sm = R₂/X₂, then falls to zero at s = 0 (N = Ns). Stable region is from sm to 0, with a near-linear part around full-load slip. Increasing rotor resistance moves sm towards 1 without altering Tmax.

Generating region (s < 0): if the rotor is driven above Ns by a prime mover, slip is negative, the torque reverses and the machine delivers power to the supply (induction generator). Braking region (s > 1): if the rotor is driven opposite to the field (e.g. by interchanging two stator leads), speed is negative, s > 1; the torque opposes rotation and the machine acts as a brake (plugging), drawing power from both the supply and the shaft. The torque–speed curve is the torque–slip curve mirrored with speed N = Ns(1 − s), plotted from −N to above Ns.

Also sketches of squirrel-cage bars with end rings and slip-ring rotor with brushes and rheostat.

rubric.point: Need for starters: high starting current 5–7 times full load, low starting torque
DOL starter: construction with contactor, start/stop buttons, overload relay, circuit diagram
DOL starter working and protection (NVC, thermal OLR)
Star-delta starter circuit/switch diagram
Star-delta working with ratio V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 and current/torque reduction to 1/3
Applications/limitations

answer: Need for starters. At starting the rotor is stationary, s = 1, the rotor emf and current are maximum and the stator draws a starting current of 5–7 times the full-load value (like a short-circuited transformer). This causes a large voltage dip on the supply, can trip other equipment and overheat windings, though starting torque is low. A starter limits the starting current by reducing the voltage applied to the stator (not applicable to DOL).

Direct-On-Line (DOL) starter. Connects the motor directly to full supply voltage. Construction: a 3-pole contactor (coil with 'start' (NO) and 'stop' (NC) push buttons), a thermal overload relay in series with the motor, and fuses/MCB. Used for small motors (up to about 5 kW).

DOL working. Pressing START energises the contactor coil from the supply; the main contacts close and connect the stator to the 3-phase supply, and an auxiliary hold-on contact (in parallel with START) keeps the coil energised. Pressing STOP breaks the coil circuit and the motor stops. Protections: no-volt release (the contactor drops out on supply failure and the motor does not restart automatically); thermal overload relay trips the NC contact in the coil circuit when current is excessive.

Star-delta (Y-Δ) starter. Used for motors whose stator is normally connected in delta, with all six winding terminals brought out. It uses a triple-pole double-throw (TPDT) switch (or three contactors with timer) to connect the stator in star during starting and then in delta for running.

Y-Δ working. In the START position the windings are in star, so each phase gets VL/√3 (58% of line voltage). Starting phase current falls to 1/√3, and the line current in star is IL(Y) = VL/(√3 Z); in delta it would be IL(Δ) = √3VL/Z, hence IL(Y)/IL(Δ) = 1/3. After the motor reaches about 80% of speed, the switch is thrown to RUN (delta) and the windings get full line voltage. Starting torque ∝ V² so it also falls to 1/3 of the direct-on-line value.

Comparison and use. DOL: simple, cheap, high current (5–7 IFL), small motors. Y-Δ: reduces current to about 2–2.5 IFL, cheap, but low starting torque and requires 6-terminal delta motors with no-load or light-load starting (fans, pumps, machine tools). For larger motors autotransformer starters or rotor resistance starters (slip-ring motors) are used.

rubric.point: Single-phase winding gives a pulsating flux = two equal and opposite rotating fluxes (Φ<sub>m</sub>/2 each)
Torque curves of forward and backward fields; zero net torque at standstill
Conclusion: not self-starting but runs in either direction if started
Split-phase starting (main and auxiliary windings, centrifugal switch) with phasor diagram
Capacitor-start (and capacitor-run / two-value) motor
Shaded-pole motor
Typical applications

answer: Double-revolving field theory. A single-phase winding carries alternating current and produces a pulsating (alternating) flux Φ = Φm cos ωt along a fixed axis. This is resolved into two rotating fluxes, each of constant magnitude Φm/2 and rotating at synchronous speed Ns in opposite directions: forward field Φf and backward field Φb. Indeed (Φm/2)[cos(ωt) + cos(ωt)] along the axis and the quadrature parts (Φm/2)(± sin ωt) cancel.

Why not self-starting. Each field acts on the rotor like the RMF of a 3-phase motor and produces its own torque: Tf (forward) and Tb (backward, negative). At standstill the slip is s = 1 for the forward field and 2 − s = 1 for the backward field, so |Tf| = |Tb| and the net starting torque T = Tf − Tb = 0. The motor merely hums at standstill. If, however, the rotor is given a push in either direction, the corresponding field's torque exceeds the other (forward slip small, backward slip near 2) and the motor accelerates in that direction. So it needs a method to create a rotating field at start.

Split-phase motor. The stator has a main (running) winding of low resistance and high reactance and an auxiliary (starting) winding of high resistance and low reactance, 90° apart in space. The currents Im and Ia differ in phase by about 30°, giving a weak rotating field and a starting torque of 1–1.5 times full load. A centrifugal switch disconnects the starting winding at 70–80% of speed. Used for fans, washing machines, small pumps.

Capacitor-start motor. A capacitor (electrolytic) in series with the auxiliary winding gives a phase difference of nearly 90° between Ia and Im, so a large starting torque (3–4.5 times full load) is produced; the capacitor and winding are cut out by the centrifugal switch. Capacitor-run (permanent split capacitor) – the capacitor and auxiliary winding remain in circuit, giving quiet, smooth running and better power factor but lower starting torque (ceiling fans). Capacitor-start capacitor-run (two-value) uses both a starting and a running capacitor for the best performance (compressors, refrigerators).

Shaded-pole motor. The stator has salient poles, each with a shading ring (a short-circuited copper ring) around about one-third of the pole face. Flux in the shaded portion lags the flux in the unshaded part, creating a moving field from the unshaded to the shaded part, which gives a small starting torque. Simple, rugged, cheap, but low torque, low efficiency and fixed direction of rotation. Used for table fans, hair dryers, small blowers (up to about 100 W).

rubric.point: Classification of alternators (salient pole vs cylindrical rotor; prime mover; horizontal/vertical)
Construction of salient-pole and cylindrical-rotor alternators with applications
Working principle of alternator and frequency f = PN<sub>s</sub>/120
Principle of operation of synchronous motor (rotor locking with RMF)
Not self-starting reason and methods of starting
Differences between induction and synchronous motors (at least 4)

answer: Classification of alternators. (i) By rotor construction: salient-pole (projecting poles) and non-salient (cylindrical/round rotor). (ii) By prime mover: steam/gas-turbine driven, hydro-turbine driven, diesel/engine driven. (iii) By axis: horizontal or vertical shaft. (iv) By output: single-phase or three-phase.

Constructional details. Stator (armature): laminated core with slots carrying the 3-phase winding. Salient-pole rotor: projecting poles with field coils bolted to a spider on a large-diameter, short-axial-length rotor; many poles (low speed 100–400 rpm); with damper windings; used with hydro-turbines and diesel engines. Cylindrical rotor: smooth solid steel forging with slots carrying distributed field winding; small diameter, long axial length; 2 or 4 poles (1500–3000 rpm); mechanically strong at high speed; used with steam and gas turbines (turbo-alternators). The field is excited by DC through slip rings from an exciter.

Principle of an alternator. DC fed to the rotor field gives a flux; the prime mover rotates it at Ns and the flux cuts the stator conductors, inducing an alternating EMF of frequency f = PNs/120 in each phase (Faraday's law); the three phase windings 120° apart yield a balanced 3-phase EMF E = 4.44 Kw f Φ Tph.

Synchronous motor – principle. The 3-phase stator carries a 3-phase supply and produces an RMF of speed Ns. When the DC-excited rotor is rotating at (or near) Ns, its poles lock magnetically with the opposite poles of the rotating stator field and the rotor is dragged round at exactly synchronous speed with the torque angle δ depending on the load. Speed is constant (Ns = 120f/P) from no-load to full-load, and it can run at lagging, unity or leading p.f. by changing the field excitation (over-excited = leading, used for p.f. correction as a synchronous condenser).

Not self-starting. At standstill, the stator field rotates at Ns but the rotor, due to its inertia, cannot instantly accelerate; the stator poles pass the rotor poles so fast that the average torque in half cycle is attractive and in the next repulsive, so net starting torque is zero. Starting methods: (i) bring the rotor close to synchronous speed with a small auxiliary motor and then synchronise; (ii) as an induction motor using damper (amortisseur) windings on the pole faces, with the DC field applied once speed reaches about 95%; (iii) using a variable-frequency supply.

Comparison. Synchronous motor: runs at constant Ns (no slip), needs DC excitation, not self-starting, can operate at any p.f. (lagging/unity/leading), costlier, air gap larger. Induction motor: speed slightly less than Ns (slip), no separate excitation, self-starting, always lagging p.f., cheaper, rugged, small air gap.

rubric.point: (a) Neat single-line diagram: generating station → step-up transformer → transmission → receiving station → distribution → consumer
(a) Explanation of each stage (generation, primary/secondary transmission, primary/secondary distribution) with function
(b) Table of standard voltage levels in India (generation, transmission, distribution)
(b) Economic advantages of high-voltage transmission (I = P/(√3 V cosφ), reduced I²R loss, conductor saving, regulation, capacity)

answer: (a) Layout of an electric power system. Electrical energy is generated at a central generating station, stepped up, transmitted over long distances at high voltage, stepped down at substations and finally distributed to consumers at utilisation voltage.
1. Generating station: thermal, hydro, nuclear or renewable plant; alternators generate 3-phase AC at 11 kV (up to 33 kV for large units), 50 Hz.
2. Step-up substation: a transformer raises the generation voltage to the primary transmission voltage (132/220/400 kV) to reduce current and losses.
3. Primary transmission: overhead lines carry bulk power at 220/400 kV to the grid receiving stations.
4. Secondary transmission: at the receiving substation voltage is stepped down to 132/66 kV and power is carried to secondary (grid) substations near load centres.
5. Primary distribution: at the distribution substation voltage is reduced to 33 kV/11 kV and fed to large industrial consumers and to distribution transformers.

6. Secondary distribution: pole/plinth-mounted distribution transformers step down 11 kV to 415 V (3-phase, 4-wire) / 230 V (single phase) for residential, commercial and small industrial consumers through service mains.

Single-line diagram (drawn with one line for the three phases): Generator (11 kV) → Step-up transformer (11/220 kV) → 220 kV transmission line → Step-down transformer (220/66 kV) → 66 kV secondary transmission → Substation (66/11 kV) → 11 kV feeders → Distribution transformer (11 kV/415 V) → Consumers.
(b) Standard voltage levels in India (table):
AC generation: 11 kV, 13.8 kV, 15.75 kV (up to 33 kV).
Primary transmission: 220 kV, 400 kV, 765 kV (EHV).
Secondary transmission: 132 kV, 66 kV.
Primary distribution: 33 kV, 11 kV (also 6.6 kV).
Secondary distribution: 415 V three-phase line, 230 V single-phase phase-to-neutral.
Economic advantages of high-voltage transmission. For a given power P = √3 V I cosφ, the line current is I = P/(√3 V cosφ), so I ∝ 1/V.
(i) Line loss = 3I²R ∝ 1/V²; doubling the voltage cuts the I²R loss to one quarter, so efficiency is higher.
(ii) For the same loss, conductor cross-section a ∝ 1/V²; volume of copper/aluminium (and its cost) falls sharply, and lighter towers suffice.
(iii) Voltage drop IR is smaller, so regulation is better and longer distances can be covered.

(iv) Greater power-carrying capacity per circuit and fewer circuits/right-of-way needed. Limits: insulation, tower and substation costs and corona rise with V, so an economic voltage is chosen (Kelvin's law).

(a)(ii) MCB: construction (bimetal strip for overload, solenoid/magnetic trip for short circuit, arc chute), working and applications
(a)(iii) ELCB: working on residual-current (RCCB, core-balance CT) or voltage principle, trip current 30 mA, applications
(a)(iv) MCCB: construction (moulded case, thermal-magnetic or electronic trip), working and applications
(b) Comparison table of MCB, ELCB and MCCB on principle, ratings and protection

answer: (a)(i) Switch Fuse Unit (SFU). A switch and a fuse (HRC cartridge type) housed together in a metal enclosure with a quick-make quick-break handle. Principle: the fuse element melts (I²Rt heating) on overload or short circuit and breaks the circuit, while the switch is used for manual on/off and isolation. Ratings: 16 A to 1250 A, 415 V. Uses: main/incoming control of industrial and commercial distribution boards, motor feeders. Drawback: fuse must be replaced after operating.

(ii) Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB). Construction: moulded insulating case, fixed and moving contacts, operating toggle, bimetallic strip (thermal trip), solenoid/electromagnet with plunger (magnetic trip) and an arc chute with splitter plates. Working: on overload the bimetal heats, bends and releases the latch after an inverse-time delay; on short circuit the solenoid pulls the plunger instantly and trips the contacts; the arc is stretched and cooled in the arc chute. Resettable, no replacement needed. Ratings: 0.5 A to 63 A (up to 125 A), breaking capacity up to 10 kA; types B, C, D (trip curves). Used in homes, offices and final sub-circuits for lighting and sockets.

(iii) Earth Leakage Circuit Breaker (ELCB). It detects earth-leakage/fault current. Modern current-operated ELCB (RCCB/RCD): phase and neutral pass through a core-balance current transformer; in healthy condition Iphase = Ineutral and the net flux is zero. If leakage to earth occurs, the residual current produces flux, induces an EMF in the sensing coil and operates a trip relay, opening the contacts in about 30 ms. Sensitivity: 30 mA (human protection), 100/300 mA (fire protection). Older voltage-ELCB senses the voltage on the earth wire (trip above ~50 V). Applications: bathrooms, kitchens, pumps, domestic and commercial buildings for protection against electric shock and fire. It does not protect against overload or short circuit unless combined (RCBO).

(iv) Moulded Case Circuit Breaker (MCCB). Heavy-duty breaker in a moulded insulating case with a toggle handle, arc chutes, and a trip unit: thermal (bimetal) for overload and magnetic for short circuit (electronic trip in advanced types) with adjustable settings. Ratings 63 A–1600 A (up to 2500 A), breaking capacity 20–100 kA. Used for main incoming/outgoing feeders, motors, capacitor banks, industrial panels.
(b) Comparison:
Principle: MCB – bimetal + electromagnet; ELCB – residual current (core-balance) or earth voltage; MCCB – thermal-magnetic/electronic trip.
Current rating: MCB up to 63/125 A; ELCB 25–100 A (30 mA to 300 mA sensitivity); MCCB 63–1600 A or more.
Breaking capacity: MCB ≤ 10 kA; MCCB 20–100 kA.
Protection: MCB – overload and short circuit; ELCB – earth leakage/shock only; MCCB – overload and short circuit (adjustable), some with earth-fault.
Adjustability: MCB fixed; MCCB adjustable; ELCB fixed sensitivity.
Use: MCB – final circuits; ELCB – shock protection; MCCB – main feeders and industry.

rubric.point: (a) Importance of earthing: protection from shock, equipotential, fault current path to operate protective device, fire prevention
(a) Hazards of ungrounded equipment: touch voltage, shock, fire, equipment damage
(b)(i) Pipe earthing: diagram with labels and installation details
(b)(ii) Plate earthing: diagram with labels and installation details
(b) Reason for charcoal and salt (low resistance, moisture retention, corrosion protection)

answer: (a) Importance of earthing. Earthing is connecting the non-current-carrying metal parts of equipment (body, frame, enclosure) and the neutral of the system to the general mass of earth through a low-resistance conductor.

Necessity: (1) Safety of persons – if insulation fails, the body is held at near earth potential, so touch voltage is low and shock is avoided. (2) Fault current gets a low-impedance path to earth, so the fuse/MCB/ELCB operates quickly and isolates the supply. (3) Maintains equipotential surfaces, protects against lightning and static charges. (4) Prevents fire from leakage currents and stabilises voltage of healthy phases during faults.

Hazards of ungrounded equipment: a fault between live conductor and metal body keeps the body at supply voltage (230 V) so any person touching it gets a severe or fatal shock; no fault current flows to trip protection so the fault persists; risk of fire/sparking, damage to equipment and loss of life or property.

(b)(i) Pipe earthing. A galvanised iron (GI) pipe of 38–50 mm diameter and 2–3 m length with holes in its lower part is driven vertically into the ground (in a pit, moist soil). A funnel is fixed at the top (reached through a masonry/cast-iron cover chamber) for pouring water. Around the pipe, alternate layers of charcoal and common salt (or coke and salt) about 15 cm thick are filled. The earth wire (GI strip/wire) is bolted to the pipe by a nut-bolt and connected to the equipment body. Water is poured periodically (once or twice a week in summer) to keep the soil moist. Resistance should be below ~1–5 Ω. Suited to small installations and houses.

(ii) Plate earthing. A copper plate (60 cm × 60 cm × 3.15 mm) or GI plate (60 × 60 cm × 6.3 mm) is buried vertically in a pit at 3 m depth with its face vertical, surrounded by alternate layers of charcoal and salt (about 15 cm). A GI pipe of 19 mm diameter with funnel is led from the top for watering. The earth wire is bolted to the plate with two bolts and a cover/inspection chamber is provided at the top. Used for substations and large installations where larger surface area and low resistance are needed.

Why charcoal and salt? (1) Salt in solution lowers the soil resistivity, giving better conductivity around the electrode. (2) Charcoal absorbs and retains moisture, keeping the soil damp for long. (3) Charcoal also protects the electrode from corrosion and increases the effective contact surface, so earth resistance remains low and stable.
formulas: Earth resistance should be ≤ 1–5 Ω (small installations), ≤ 1 Ω (substations)

rubric.point: (a) Definition and electrochemical differences of primary vs secondary cells with examples
(b) Classification of secondary batteries by chemistry (Lead-Acid, Ni-Cd, Li-ion) with brief features
(b) Lead-acid charging and discharging reactions at anode, cathode and overall
(b) Advantages and disadvantages of lead-acid battery
(c) Specifications: Ah capacity, energy density, cycle life, C-rating, self-discharge and their selection significance

answer: (a) Primary cells convert chemical energy to electrical energy through an irreversible reaction; once reactants are consumed the cell is discarded (e.g. dry Leclanché cell, alkaline, lithium coin cell). Secondary cells (storage batteries) undergo reversible electrochemical reactions: after discharge they can be recharged by passing current in the reverse direction, restoring the active materials (e.g. lead-acid, Ni-Cd, Li-ion).

Difference: in primary cells the electrode reactions cannot be reversed, they have higher energy density and lower cost per cell and are used in low-drain devices; secondary cells have rechargeable electrode materials, lower internal resistance, can supply high currents and have thousands of cycles.

(b) Classification of secondary batteries: (i) Lead-acid – Pb/PbO2, dilute H2SO4, 2.0 V per cell, cheap, high current (automobile, UPS, inverter). (ii) Nickel-cadmium – NiOOH positive, Cd negative, KOH electrolyte, 1.2 V per cell, long life, tolerates deep discharge (emergency lighting, tools); cadmium is toxic. (iii) Lithium-ion – lithium-metal-oxide cathode, graphite anode, lithium salt in organic solvent, 3.6–3.7 V, high energy density, light weight (mobiles, laptops, EVs).

Lead-acid reactions. Discharging: Anode (negative plate): Pb + SO42− → PbSO4 + 2e−. Cathode (positive plate): PbO2 + 4H+ + SO42− + 2e− → PbSO4 + 2H2O. Overall: Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 → 2PbSO4 + 2H2O. The electrolyte becomes dilute (specific gravity falls from ≈1.28 to ≈1.12) and cell voltage falls.

Charging (reverse): 2PbSO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Pb + PbO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. PbSO<sub>4</sub> on the negative plate is reduced to spongy Pb, on the positive plate oxidised to PbO<sub>2</sub>; acid concentration and voltage rise (gassing near full charge).

Advantages: low cost, high surge current, simple and reliable, easily recyclable, low internal resistance. Disadvantages: heavy and bulky, low energy density (30–40 Wh/kg), limited cycle life (300–1500), needs maintenance (water topping), acid fumes and hydrogen gas, sulphation if left discharged, lead toxicity.

(c) Selection specifications. Ampere-hour capacity: charge it can deliver at the rated discharge rate (Ah = I × t) – decides backup time. Energy density (Wh/kg or Wh/L): determines size and weight. Cycle life: number of charge-discharge cycles before capacity falls to 80% – decides life-cycle cost. C-rating: charge/discharge rate relative to capacity (1C for a 100 Ah battery = 100 A); limits permissible current. Self-discharge rate: loss of charge on standby per month (lead-acid 3–5%, Li-ion 1–2%, Ni-Cd 15–20%) – important for standby systems. Others: voltage, temperature range, cost, depth of discharge.

rubric.point: Classification of wires (single/multi-strand, PVC, VIR, TRS, CTS) with uses
Types of cables (PVC, XLPE, armoured, flexible, coaxial, single/multi-core) with uses
Labelled sectional diagram of an armoured power cable
Function and material of conductor, insulation, bedding, armour and serving

answer: Wires are single bare or insulated conductors; cables consist of one or more insulated conductors covered by common protective sheath. Conductor materials: copper (higher conductivity) and aluminium (cheaper, lighter).

Types of wires in internal wiring: (i) VIR (vulcanised India rubber) – obsolete; (ii) PVC-insulated wires (single-core, 1.5–6 mm²) in conduit – most common, FR/FRLS types for safety; (iii) CTS/TRS (cab-tyre/tough-rubber-sheathed) wire in batten wiring; (iv) flexible multi-strand wire for appliances and portable use; (v) lead-sheathed and enamelled winding wires for machines.

Types of cables: (i) PVC cables (up to 1.1 kV) for house and building wiring; (ii) XLPE (cross-linked polyethylene) cables, 1.1 kV to 33 kV and more, higher temperature rating (90 °C); (iii) armoured power cables for underground/outdoor laying; (iv) paper-insulated lead-covered (PILC) cables for HV; (v) coaxial and communication cables; (vi) flexible, welding and submersible cables. They may be single-core, two-, three-, 3½- or four-core.
Construction of an armoured cable (from inside to outside):
1. Conductor: stranded copper or aluminium (circular or sector-shaped) – stranding gives flexibility and carries the load current.
2. Insulation: PVC or XLPE (or impregnated paper) over each core – withstands the working voltage and insulates the cores from each other; cores are identified by colour (red, yellow, blue, black).
3. Bedding: a layer of PVC/jute/hessian tape over the laid-up cores (with fillers) – gives a circular shape and protects the insulation from damage by armour.
4. Armour: galvanised steel wires (or steel tape) wound over the bedding – gives mechanical strength and protection from impact, crushing and rodents; also provides earth path.
5. Serving (outer sheath): a final PVC or compounded jute layer over armour – protects armour against moisture, corrosion and chemical attack.
Applications: underground and outdoor distribution, industrial feeders and motor connections, where mechanical stress is expected.

rubric.point: (a) Buck converter circuit diagram (source, switch, diode, L, C, load)
(a) Operation in switch ON/OFF modes with waveforms
(a) Output voltage V<sub>o</sub> = D V<sub>s</sub> with inductor volt-second balance
(b) Single-phase bridge VSI circuit and working with gate sequence and output waveform
(b) Differences between single-phase and three-phase inverters

answer: (a) DC-DC Buck (step-down) converter. Circuit: DC source Vs in series with a controlled switch S (MOSFET/IGBT) → node with a freewheeling diode D connected to ground (cathode at node) → series inductor L → output capacitor C in parallel with load R.
Mode 1 (S ON, 0 < t < DT): the diode is reverse biased, the source feeds the inductor and load; inductor voltage vL = Vs − Vo so the inductor current rises linearly and energy is stored in L.

Mode 2 (S OFF, DT < t < T): the inductor opposes the fall of current, the diode conducts (freewheels) and L feeds the load; vL = −Vo and iL falls linearly. The capacitor keeps the output ripple small.

Output voltage (continuous conduction): average inductor voltage over a period is zero (volt-second balance): (Vs − Vo)DT = Vo(1 − D)T, so Vo = D Vs, where D = Ton/T is the duty ratio (0 < D < 1). Hence Vo < Vs – step-down. Ripple current ΔIL = Vo(1 − D)/(fL). Used in SMPS, mobile chargers and battery chargers.

(b) Single-phase bridge VSI. Four switches S1–S4 (IGBT/MOSFET each with an antiparallel feedback diode) form two legs (S1, S4 and S3, S2), fed from a DC source Vdc, with the load connected between the mid-points of the legs.

Operation (square-wave): for 0 < t < T/2, S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are ON, so v<sub>o</sub> = +V<sub>dc</sub>; for T/2 < t < T, S<sub>3</sub> and S<sub>4</sub> are ON, so v<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>dc</sub>. Switches in the same leg are never ON together (dead-time) to avoid short circuit of the source. The output is a square wave of amplitude ±V<sub>dc</sub> at the frequency set by the gate pulses. The feedback diodes carry load current when it lags the voltage (inductive load).
RMS output V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>; fundamental rms = 0.9 V<sub>dc</sub> (4V<sub>dc</sub>/(π√2)). Output contains odd harmonics (3rd, 5th,…) which are reduced by filters or PWM control.

Single-phase vs three-phase inverter: Single-phase – 4 switches (bridge), single AC output, ±Vdc square wave, used for small loads (UPS, home inverters), higher harmonics and pulsating power. Three-phase – 6 switches (3 legs), three outputs 120° apart, line voltage 6-step waveform, rated for higher power (motor drives, grid), lower harmonic content, smoother torque and constant power flow, smaller DC filter.

answer: (a) Given: Lamps 10 W, 20 W, 30 W working 1 h, 2 h, 3 h daily; 30 days; tariff Rs. 10/kWh. Energy = Power × time.
Daily energy: lamp 1 = 10 × 1 = 10 Wh; lamp 2 = 20 × 2 = 40 Wh; lamp 3 = 30 × 3 = 90 Wh. Total per day = 10 + 40 + 90 = 140 Wh = 0.14 kWh.
Monthly energy = 0.14 × 30 = 4.2 kWh (units).

Daily energy = 1.5 kW × 3 h = 4.5 kWh.
Monthly energy = 4.5 × 30 = 135 kWh.
